kits.familyName: Working well with people who are different from you
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}, on a team where people have different personalities, backgrounds and ways of working.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you work with coworkers whose styles and backgrounds differ from yours.
detail: It is the middle of the afternoon.
pressure: {coworker3} says it is not worth the trouble.
You are in a hurry to finish.

tiers.1: A remark that makes a coworker uncomfortable is raised directly and privately.
tiers.2: Do not guess what a silence means; ask.
tiers.3: Differences in style are handled with a format that works for both people.
tiers.4: Reasonable requests that keep the work covered can be met.
tiers.5: Using a person's name correctly is a basic sign of respect and can follow other fixes.

fact: {coworker} joked about how you speak, and you felt uncomfortable, though it was not clear that {coworker} meant harm.
issues.short: the joke about how you speak
issues.action: Tell {coworker} privately that the joke bothered you and ask them to stop.
issues.brief: tell {coworker} privately and ask them to stop
issues.reason: A private, calm request gives {coworker} the chance to change without an audience.
issues.lesson: Raise a remark that bothers you directly and privately.

shortcut.text: Laugh along and then avoid {coworker} from now on.
shortcut.why: Avoiding {coworker} leaves the problem in place and hurts the working relationship.
shortcut.mis: Staying silent makes the problem go away.

clear: You already told {coworker} privately that the joke bothered you, and it stopped.

fact: {coworker} did not answer your invitation to the team lunch, so you assumed they were not interested, though they may not have seen it.
issues.action: Ask {coworker} directly and offer another way to share plans.
issues.reason: A silence can mean many things, including that a message was missed.
issues.lesson: Ask instead of assuming what a coworker's silence means.

shortcut.text: Stop inviting {coworker}, since they seem uninterested.
shortcut.why: An assumption can leave a coworker out for a reason that was never true.

clear: You already asked {coworker} about the team lunch and they said they missed the message.
issues.done: the lunch question is already asked

fact: {coworker} likes to talk ideas through aloud while you prefer to think quietly first, and meetings feel tense.
issues.action: Suggest a format with a short quiet thinking time and then open discussion.
issues.brief: suggest quiet thinking time and then discussion
issues.reason: A shared format lets both styles contribute without either person being told to change who they are.
issues.lesson: Handle style differences with a format that works for both people.

shortcut.text: Tell {coworker} to talk less in meetings.
shortcut.why: It asks one person to change, and it treats a working style as a fault.
shortcut.mis: One person's style is the right one.

clear: You and {coworker} already agreed on a meeting format that suits you both.
issues.done: the meeting format is already agreed

fact: A coworker wants a day off that matters to their family, and {lead|the} says swaps are fine if the work stays covered.
issues.short: the coworker's request for the day off
issues.action: Offer to swap shifts, as {lead|the} described.
issues.reason: {Lead|the} has already said swaps are allowed, so you can help without any extra approval.
issues.lesson: Help meet a reasonable request when the rules already allow a way.

shortcut.text: Tell them everyone works the schedule as posted.
shortcut.why: {Lead|the} has said swaps are allowed, so the schedule is not fixed.

clear: {Coworker} already arranged a shift swap for a day that matters to their family.
issues.done: the day off is already arranged

fact: You keep mispronouncing a new coworker's name, and they have corrected you twice.
issues.action: Ask them to say it again, practice it, and use it correctly.
issues.brief: ask for the name again and practice it
issues.reason: Using someone's name correctly shows that you value them, and practicing is a small effort.
issues.lesson: Learn to say a coworker's name correctly instead of changing it.

shortcut.text: Use a nickname you find easier, since they seem friendly.
shortcut.brief: use a nickname you find easier
shortcut.why: Replacing a name without being asked can make a coworker feel unseen.
shortcut.mis: A friendly coworker will not mind a changed name.

proceed.text: Carry on with your regular work, since nothing here needs action.
proceed.why: Each of these situations involves working respectfully with a coworker who is different from you.
proceed.lesson: Working across differences means asking, speaking directly and finding ways that suit everyone.

generic.text: Ask {coworker2} what they usually do and copy that.
generic.why: A coworker's habit is not the written guide, and it may be out of date.
generic.mis: Common practice is the same as the rule.

generic.text: Wait until {lead|the} brings it up before you act.
generic.why: The guide applies to you now, and waiting leaves the problem in place.
generic.mis: Someone else will raise it if it matters.

overcaution.text: Never speak to {coworker} again so there can be no more misunderstandings.
overcaution.why: The concern is a specific misunderstanding. Cutting off contact makes teamwork impossible.

setup: You and a coworker disagree about how to run team meetings.

steps.text: Ask your coworker how they like meetings to run
Explain how you like them to run
Propose a format that suits both
Try the format at the next meeting

rel: A format builds on what both of you said.
Try the format once it is agreed.
A shared proposal considers your coworker's view too.
process.lesson: Hear both preferences, propose a shared format, then try it.

title: Notes on working with different people
intro: You are reading a coworker's draft advice on working with people who are different.
prompt: Which line gives advice that would make working relationships worse?
doc.lesson: Good teamwork asks questions, speaks directly and adjusts the way the team works.

lines.text: Ask a coworker what their silence means before you decide.

bad.text: Decide a coworker is not interested when they do not reply.
bad.why: A missed message or busy day can explain a silence.

lines.text: Raise a remark that bothers you directly and privately.
lines.fine: Gives the person a chance to change.

bad.text: Avoid a coworker who bothers you instead of raising it.
bad.why: The problem stays and the relationship suffers.

lines.text: Find a meeting format that works for different styles.

bad.text: Tell the louder coworker to talk less so meetings feel calmer.
bad.why: It treats one style as the problem when both can fit in a shared format.

lines.text: Learn to say a coworker's name correctly.

review.notes: Respect and communication only; no group is described by traits, and no cultural or legal rules are stated. Each difference is an individual preference stated in the scenario. Tiers: remarks, assumptions, styles, requests, names.
